_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I: Pishdadian kings Gaiumart to Zahhak. Passages are modern-English paraphrase, each with mandatory paraphrase note.

title.en: Kaiumars, the First King of Mankind
title.zh: 蓋尤馬爾斯：人類第一王

region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Gaiumart, secs. 1-2

summary.en: The legendary record says Kaiumars first wore the crown among men, ruling from a mountain when the sun stood in Aries; his people wore leopard-skins and the arts of life began under him. Secretly Ahriman envied him and set his monstrous son against the king's beloved heir Siyamak, and the Black Div tore the young prince apart on the field of battle.
summary.zh: 傳說記載蓋尤馬爾斯首戴王冠，太陽在白羊座之時於山上稱王；其民披豹皮，生活技藝始於其朝。阿赫里曼暗中嫉妒，遣其怪異之子攻擊王之愛子西亞馬克，黑魔於陣前將王子撕裂，王國為之哀慟。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Zoroastrian figures rendered as medieval Persian legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The record of the first days has perished; yet the compiler of ancient legend says that Gaiumart first devised crown and throne and was a Shah. This order and grace and lustre came to earth when the sun was dominant in Aries and shone so brightly that the world grew young. Its lord dwelt at first upon a mountain, and thence his throne and fortune rose; he and all his troop wore leopard-skins, and under him the arts of life began, for food and dress were still in their infancy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had a son named Siyamak, ambitious as his sire, his father's life and joy. Only in secret did the Shah have an enemy: wicked Ahriman, led by envy, who had a son like a fearless savage wolf and a host of warriors behind him. The son assembled that host and resolved to win the great Shah's throne, and he filled the world with clamour. Who told Gaiumart of the foe? The blessed Suriish appeared in fairy form, bedight in leopard-skin, and told the king what his enemies were plotting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When host met host, Siyamak came unarmed to grapple with the son of Ahriman; that horrible Black Div clutched at him, bent down the prince of lofty stature, and rent him open. Gaiumart left his throne, wailed aloud, tore his face and body with his nails, and all the soldiers wept as birds and beasts flocked to the mountain with doleful cries. After a year the blessed Suriish came again: lament no more, said he, collect thy troops and turn thy foemen into dust. So the aged king girt himself for vengeance night and day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Hushang Wins Iron, Canals, and Seed from the Rocks
title.zh: 胡尚格：鐵器、溝渠與五穀

region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Hushang sec. 1

summary.en: Hushang, grandson of Kaiumars and son of the slain Siyamak, reigns forty years as a just Shah who civilises the world. He is the first to smelt iron from the rock and invent smithing, cutting axes, saws, and mattocks; he digs irrigation canals, and where men had lived on fruit and leaves they learn to sow, reap, and plant.
summary.zh: 胡尚格為西亞馬克之子、蓋尤馬爾斯之孫，公正治世四十年：首自岩石煉鐵，發明鍛造，造斧鋸鎬；鑿渠引水；昔日人類以果葉為生，自此學會播種收穫，安居其位。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The blessed Siyamak had left a son, his grandsire's minister, a prince named Hushang, a name implying sense and wisdom. Hushang, a just and prudent sovereign, assumed his grandsire's crown and for forty years heaven turned above him. I lord it over the seven climes, he said, victorious everywhere; my word is law, I practise bounteousness and equity; so hath God willed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He civilised the world and filled the surface of the earth with justice. He was the first to deal with minerals and win iron from the rock by craft; he gained more knowledge and, inventing smithing, made axes, saws, and mattocks. Next he turned to irrigation by canals and ducts, and grace made the labour short. As knowledge grew men sowed and reaped and planted, each produced the loaf whereof he ate, and kept his station. Till then men had lived on fruit in poor estate and clothed themselves in leaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: How Hushang Found Fire and Founded the Feast of Sada
title.zh: 胡尚格取火與薩達節之起源

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Hushang sec. 2

summary.en: Hushang hurled a stone at a fire-breathing serpent on a mountain; it missed and struck a flint, and the sparks revealed fire hidden in stone. Hushang praised God for the radiant gift, taught men to worship it, made a great blaze with his people, and held the feast called Sada, which remains his memorial. He then domesticated ox, ass, and sheep for toil and produce.
summary.zh: 胡尚格於山中擲石擊蛇，石落燧石迸出火星，揭示石中藏火。他感謝神賜光焰，教人崇火，夜聚族人舉火設宴，是為薩達節，永為其紀念。其後馴服牛驢羊供役使，取其毛革而澤被萬民。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; etiological myth for the Sada festival and fire-cult. No living community restriction.

passages.text: One day Hushang reached a mountain with his men and saw afar a long swift dusky form with eyes like pools of blood and jaws whose smoke bedimmed the world. Hushang the wary seized a stone, advanced, and hurled it royally. The world-consuming worm escaped, the stone struck on a larger one, and both were shivered; sparks issued and the centres flashed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fire came from its stony hiding-place, and the worldlord offered praise for such a radiant gift. He made of fire a cynosure: this lustre is divine, he said, and thou, if wise, must worship it. That night he made a mighty blaze and stood around it with his men and held the feast called Sada; that bright festival remaineth as his memorial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: By grace and kingly power he domesticated ox, ass, and sheep and turned them to good use: pair them, he said, use them for toil, enjoy their produce, and provide therewith your taxes. He slew the furry rovers for their skins, so that squirrel, ermine, fox, and sable clothed the talkers; he gave and spent freely, and when he passed he took naught with him but repute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tahmuras, the Binder of the Div

region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Tahmuras

summary.en: Tahmuras son of Hushang invents spinning, drapery, and falconry, then binds the rebellious divs and their patron Ahriman with spells and rides him horsewise around the world. The captured demons beg their lives, promising a new and fruitful art in return, and teach him thirty scripts, among them Pahlavi, so that sounds may be delineated in writing.
summary.zh: 胡尚格之子塔胡穆拉斯（縛魔者）發明紡織與鷹獵；群魔叛亂，他以咒縛眾魔，又縛阿赫里曼如馬乘騎環行天下。被縛之魔求饒，許以新藝，遂授其三十種文字——帕拉維文在焉——聲音自此得以書寫。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. The motif 'transformation' covers Ahriman turned horsewise for riding; interpretive tag. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Hushang possessed a wise and noble son hight Tahmuras, the Binder of the Div, who took the throne and girt his loins to rule. I will restrain the Div, he said, will reign supreme, and use the useful for the common good. He sheared the flocks and men began to spin; he thus invented clothes and draperies. He chose the swiftest quadrupeds and made them feed on barley and hay, lured the shyest beasts of prey from hill and plain to obey him, and began to tame the hawk and noble falcon while men looked on amazed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Glorious with the Grace, he bound Ahriman with spells and rode him horsewise at whiles around the world. Thereat the divs rebelled and held a conclave, for their throne of gold was void. When Tahmuras was ware he girt him with Grace, took his massive mace, and advanced against the huge magician host led by the Black Div; of the foe he bound the most by spells and quelled the others with his mace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The captives bound and stricken begged their lives: destroy us not, and we will teach thee a new and fruitful art. He gave them quarter, and they taught him how to write some thirty scripts, such as the Persian, Arabic, Sughdi, Chini, and Pahlavi, and thus delineate sounds. How many better arts he explored in a reign of thirty years, yet passed away, and all his toils became his monument.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Jamshid's Crafts, Castes, and Aerial Throne
title.zh: 賈姆希德：百工、四階與凌空御座

region.zh: 帕爾斯伊斯塔赫爾（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Jamshid sec. 1

summary.en: Jamshid son of Tahmuras forges arms and silk, founds the four castes of priests, warriors, tillers, and artisans, teaches the divs to bake brick and raise baths and sanctuaries, unlocks gems and perfumes and leechcraft, and is first to cross the sea in ships. He builds a gem-inlaid throne that divs bear up to heaven, and the day is named New Year's Day — the first of Farwardin, memorial of that Shah.
summary.zh: 賈姆希德鑄兵甲、織絲綢，立祭司、戰士、農夫、工匠四階；教魔製磚築浴場聖所，發寶石香料醫道，首以舟渡海。更造鑲寶御座，魔抬升天，眾人撒寶石慶賀，是日定名歲首——法爾瓦爾丁月初一，永為其紀念。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nowruz etiology included. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Jamshid, the mighty son of Tahmuras, succeeded to his glorious father's throne and wore in kingly wise the crown of gold. His girdle was the Grace of king of kings, and all the world obeyed him; contests ceased and the age had rest. Mine is the Grace, he said, I am both king and archimage; I will restrain ill-doers and make for souls a path toward the light. He first wrought arms and opened for warriors the door of fame, fashioning iron into helmets, hauberks, breastplates, and coats of armour for man and horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then to the joy of all he founded castes for every craft: a sacerdotal caste to serve in quiet on the mountains, a military caste of lion-men to guard the royal throne, an agricultural caste of independent tillers — idleness maketh freemen slaves, quoth he — and the artizans who live by handiwork. He bade the foul divs temper earth with water and fashion moulds for bricks, laying foundations with stone and lime and raising hot baths, lofty halls, and sanctuaries. He searched the rocks for jewels — rubies, amber, silver, gold — and brought them forth by spells.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He introduced the scents men enjoy, as camphor, musk, sweet aloe, and bright rosewater; next leechcraft and the healing of the sick were secrets opened by Jamshid. He crossed the sea in ships. His wisdom achieved, he made himself a throne with what a wealth of gems inlaid, which when he willed the divs took up and bare from earth to heaven. There the Shah sat sunlike in mid air; the world assembled round his throne in wonder, and bestowed upon the day the name of New Year's Day, the first of Farwardin, which remaineth the memorial of that Shah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Jamshid Claims Godhead and Loses the Grace
title.zh: 賈姆希德僭稱神而失天恩

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Jamshid secs. 2, 4

summary.en: Spoiled by three centuries of a deathless golden age, Jamshid summons the chiefs and claims to be the Maker of the world: who adores me not is an Ahriman. The Grace departs; the court empties; day darkens to him, and though he weeps tears of blood no pardon comes. Pretenders rise, and when Zahhak seizes the crown Jamshid flees, hides a century, and is at last caught beside the sea of Chin and sawn asunder.
summary.zh: 賈姆希德享三百年不死盛世，驕而僭稱造世主：「不拜我者即阿赫里曼。」天恩遂離，朝廷空寂，日為之暗；他泣血求恕而不可得。群雄並起，扎哈克奪位，賈姆希德遁藏百年，終於秦地海濱被擒，鋸為兩半。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; transgression-of-hubris narrative. No living community restriction.

passages.text: For three centuries all the while men never looked on death; they wotted not of travail or of ill, and divs like slaves were girt to do them service. One day contemplating the throne of power Jamshid deemed that he was peerless; he knew God, but acted frowardly and turned aside in his ingratitude. He summoned all the chiefs: the world is mine, I found its properties; leechcraft hath cured the world, disease and death are stayed; they who adore me not are Ahrimans; so now all hail me as the Maker of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid secs. 1, 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereat the archmages hung their heads, perplexed to answer, and God's Grace departed from him. The world was filled with din, the Court deserted, and none who desired renown stayed in his presence. Day darkened to Jamshid; though with tears of blood he sought for pardon, Grace was not, and dread of coming evil was his lot. How saith the seer? King though thou art, serve God; great fears oppress the heart that is devoid of thankfulness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pretenders started up and the disaffected nobles levied troops; hearing that there was an awe-inspiring king of dragon-visage in Arabia, they went to Zahhak and offered fealty. Zahhak came like wind and donned the Iranian crown, and thus fell Jamshid: he fled, surrendering crown, throne, and treasure. He was in hiding for a century, but in the hundredth year he appeared one day beside the sea of Chin; Zahhak clutched him forthwith and, sawing him asunder, freed the world from him and from the fear that he inspired.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Zahhak Swears His Father's Throne to Iblis
title.zh: 扎哈克向伊布利斯立誓弑父

region.zh: 阿拉伯荒漠（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak secs. 2-3

summary.en: Iblis approaches Zahhak, the gallant but hasty son of the righteous Arab king Mardas, as a friendly monitor, wins his trust, and exacts an oath: first promise, then my story. The oath binds Zahhak to do Iblis' bidding, and the bidding is patricide — Iblis digs a masked pit in the garden-path where Mardas bathes at dawn, and the good king falls and breaks his back. Thus the abandoned son seizes the throne.
summary.zh: 伊布利斯偽作諍友接近阿拉伯賢王馬爾達斯之子扎哈克，誘其先誓後言。誓言縛其遵命行事，而命即弑父：伊布利斯於王黎明沐浴的花徑掘坑偽裝，賢王墜坑折背而亡。悖逆之子遂篡其位。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. 'Iblis' is the Muslim fiend-name folded into the older Ahriman legend; interpretive. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Mardas was a virtuous king of the desert Bedouins, just, highborn, and generous, who kept a thousand head of milch cattle and Arab steeds and grudged the milk to none. He had a son whom much he loved: Zahhak, a gallant prince but hasty. One day Iblis approached him as a friend and led his wits astray; the youth gave ear with pleasure and, all unsuspectingly, gave to Iblis heart, reason, and pure soul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tell me at once, my worthy monitor, said the youth. Iblis replied: first promise, then my story. The guileless youth swore as Iblis dictated: thy secret shall be kept, thy bidding done. Then said Iblis: shall any rule here but thyself? What profiteth a sire with such a son? The lifetime of this ancient potentate continueth; seize on his court and goods, thou shalt be king of the world if thou durst do my bidding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zahhak looked grave, for to shed his sire's blood grieved him, but Iblis told him to leave the scheming to himself; he only asked the prince's silence. In the palace was a jocund garth whither Mardas used to go at dawn to bathe him ere he prayed; the wicked Div dug in the garden-path a deep pit, masked and made it good with boughs. Ere dawn the Arab chieftain hied him thither, and as he reached the pit his fortunes fell: that good man tumbled, broke his back, and died. Thus vile and unjust Zahhak seized the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Two Cooks, Sheep's Brains, and the Birth of the Kurds
title.zh: 雙廚以羊腦代之：庫爾德人源流

region.zh: 扎哈克王宮（象徵巴比倫）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 1

summary.en: During Zahhak's thousand-year reign two youths a night are slaughtered to feed the serpents on their brains. The pious high-born Persians Irmail and Karmail learn cookery, enter the king's kitchen, and save one of every pair by mixing sheep's brains with the slain youth's; thirty a month, two hundred in all, are furnished with sheep and goats and sent desertward. Thus spring the Kurds, who dwell in woollen tents and know no settled home.
summary.zh: 扎哈克千年暴政期間，每夜殺二青年以腦飼蛇。虔誠貴族伊爾邁勒與卡爾邁勒學藝入庖，每對救一：以羊腦混入死者之腦。每月三十人，共二百人，賜羊遣往荒漠——庫爾德人由此而生，居氈帳而無定所。

sensitivity.note: Medieval etiology of the Kurds framed around human sacrifice; read as epic legend, not as ethnography. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Zahhak sat on the throne a thousand years, obeyed by all the world; through that long time the customs of the wise were out of vogue, the lusts of madmen flourished everywhere, and all virtue was despised while black art was esteemed. Each night two youths of high or lowly birth were taken to the palace by the cook, who having slaughtered them took out their brains to feed the snakes and ease the monarch's anguish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the realm were two good high-born Persians, the pious Irmail and Karmail the prescient. Talking of the lawless Shah and his hideous meals, one said: by cookery we might approach the Shah, and by our wits devise a scheme to rescue one from each pair doomed to death. They went and learned that art, became the monarch's cooks, and rejoiced in secret.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When some murderous minions of the Shah dragged two youths to them, they slew one and mingled his precious brains with sheep's, sparing the other, to whom they said: make shift to hide thyself, approach not any dwelling-place of man, thine are the wastes and heights. A worthless head thus fed the serpents, and in every month the cooks preserved from slaughter thirty youths; when the number reached two hundred they provided them with sheep and goats and sent them desertward. Thus sprang the Kurds, who know no settled home but dwell in woollen tents and fear not God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Zahhak's Dream of the Ox-Headed Mace
title.zh: 扎哈克夢見牛首狼牙棒

region.zh: 扎哈克王宮（象徵巴比倫）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 2

summary.en: Zahhak dreams that three warriors, boughs of the tree of kings, come against him; the youngest, a tall cypress of kingly face, smites him with an ox-head mace, flays him, binds his hands with his own skin, yokes his neck, and drags him in shame toward Mount Damawand. He wails from sleep; the wise archimage Zirak, forced to speak under threat of hanging, names the future destroyer: not yet born, his name is Faridun.
summary.zh: 扎哈克夢見三勇士——王族之枝——其中最幼者面如君王、身若翠柏，持牛首狼牙棒擊其首，剝其皮縛其手，加軛於頸，拖向達馬萬德山。他驚叫失色；術士齊拉克迫於王命道破天機：那尚未出生者名為法里東，將傾其王座。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; prophetic-dream motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: One longsome night Zahhak slumbered in the arms of Arnawaz and saw a vision of three warriors, boughs of the tree of kings. The youngest, who held the middle place, was a tall cypress, in face, in armour, and in mien a king. He rushed with ox-head mace to fight Zahhak, smote him upon the head, stripped off his skin, used it as a rope to bind his hands firm as a rock, placed on his neck a yoke, and dragged him in shame and anguish toward Mount Damawand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tyrant writhed and yelled; the palace of the hundred columns shook, and Arnawaz asked what he had seen. He told them every whit, then counsel was given: call both the archmages and astrologers and see if the hand that threateneth thy life is that of fairy, div, or man. When the Lamp showed o'er the hills Zahhak brought the archimages and demanded his latter end on pain of being hung alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Among them was a man wise, honest, and prescient, by name Zirak, chief of the band of archimages. Concerned but fearless, he addressed Zahhak: none is born except to die; if thou wert an iron wall yon heaven would grind thee. One will hereafter take thy throne and fling thy fortune to the ground; his name is Faridun, and he will be a royal heaven to earth. As yet he is not born, thy time of woe hath not arrived, but when his honoured mother hath borne him he will be a fruitful tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
